title: Julia
subtitle: A fast, dynamic language for science and engineering, built around multiple dispatch so that code reads like the mathematics and runs close to the speed of C.
description: Julia is a high-level, dynamically typed language designed for numerical and scientific computing. Work on it began at MIT in 2009, it was announced in 2012, and version 1.0, with its promise of stability, arrived in 2018. It was built to end the **two-language problem**, in which scientists sketch an idea in a convenient language such as Python, MATLAB or R and then rewrite the slow parts in C or Fortran. Julia compiles each function for the types it is actually called with, so a short, readable program can run at speeds close to compiled C. Its central idea, **multiple dispatch**, lets independent packages share types and functions in a way that has made its ecosystem unusually composable. It is used for differential equations and simulation, optimisation, climate and astronomy, pharmacology, economics, and machine learning research.

This course takes you from a first program to the way experienced Julia programmers work: types and control flow, functions and multiple dispatch, arrays, broadcasting and linear algebra, your own composite and parametric types, writing fast code, modules, packages and tests, macros and metaprogramming, and parallel computing, ending with a simulation project. It assumes the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience: you know what a variable, a loop and a function are. Some school algebra helps; no previous Julia, and no linear algebra beyond what the lessons explain, is needed.

To run the programs, install Julia with the official installer, **juliaup**, following the instructions at [julialang.org/downloads](https://julialang.org/downloads/); it keeps Julia up to date and lets you switch versions. Julia has no official online playground, so you work in its REPL or run scripts with `julia file.jl`. Every program marked as checked was run by Lumenary's test suite with Julia 1.13 and its standard library only; examples that use registered packages such as DataFrames or Plots are shown as plain code and explained. The lessons were drafted with AI assistance and are awaiting review by a human computer scientist.

levels.title: The core language
levels.summary: Why Julia exists and how to work in its REPL, then numbers, types and control flow, functions and multiple dispatch, and arrays, broadcasting and linear algebra.

levels.title: Building real programs
levels.summary: Your own composite and parametric types, the habits that make Julia code fast, and organising code into modules, packages and tested projects within the wider ecosystem.

levels.title: Julia as professionals use it
levels.summary: Code that writes code with expressions and macros, then threads, tasks and distributed computing, brought together in a complete simulation project.
